articles.headline: Cientos de vecinos piden frenar el derribo de seis chalés en Barreiros
articles.subtitle: Entre 300 y 400 personas, según la Guardia Civil, se concentraron ante el consistorio bajo el lema «Hai solución sen demolición» para exigir una alternativa a la orden de derribo que pesa sobre seis viviendas en Lóngara.
articles.body:
Entre 300 y 400 personas, según la Guardia Civil, se concentraron el viernes ante el consistorio de Barreiros para exigir una alternativa al derribo de seis chalés de Lóngara, sobre los que pesa una orden judicial firme. Bajo el lema «Hai solución sen demolición», los afectados reunieron a vecinos y turistas en su primera movilización pública.

El caso viene de lejos: en 2012 se declaró ilegal el acuerdo de 2002, validado entonces con licencias municipales, que segregó un terreno en seis parcelas sobre las que se construyeron las viviendas. La Axencia Galega de Protección Urbanística instó al derribo y el juzgado apremia ahora al Concello, gobernado por BNG y PSOE, a ejecutarlo bajo apercibimiento de desobediencia a la alcaldesa, Ana Ermida, que ha repetido que no delinquirá.

## La vía del Supremo

Los propietarios, que llevan veinte años litigando, confían en una resolución del Tribunal Supremo prevista para noviembre en un caso similar de Valdoviño. Si les declarara «terceros de buena fe», sostienen, el Concello debería indemnizarles —calculan tres millones de euros— y la demolición resultaría inejecutable, abriendo la puerta a regularizar las casas con un nuevo Plan Xeral de Ordenación Municipal.

«Levamos 20 anos de indefensión», resumió César Abelleira, uno de los dueños, que acusó a las administraciones de haber creado el problema. El activista de Adega Daniel López Vispo recordó la burbuja urbanística de Barreiros, donde en 2006 se concedieron licencias para unos 3.000 pisos, y cuestionó que solo estos seis chalés hayan llegado a la demolición. La protesta contó con el apoyo de representantes del PP, partido que gobernaba cuando se tramitaron las licencias.

articles.headline: Sarria estrena la Noite Meiga como Fiesta de Interés Turístico de Galicia
articles.subtitle: Decenas de personas recorrieron la villa con antorchas en la primera edición desde el reconocimiento, que este año incorporó un tramo sin ruido para personas con hipersensibilidad acústica.
articles.body:
Decenas de personas participaron el viernes en el desfile con antorchas de la Noite Meiga de Sarria, la primera edición desde que la celebración fue declarada Fiesta de Interés Turístico de Galicia. El recorrido partió de la sociedad La Unión y terminó en el parque de O Chanto, tras pasar por la calle Matías López, el bulevar de la Rúa da Liberdade y el paseo del Malecón.

Encabezados por cuatro meigas y el grupo de música de la asociación organizadora, Meigas e Trasgos, niños y mayores completaron el desfile. Como novedad de este año, una parte del recorrido se hizo en silencio para las personas con hipersensibilidad acústica. Ya por la noche actuaron en O Chanto Xosé Lois Romero & Aliboria, DeNinghures y Terrae.

## Danza en la madrugada

Los actos continúan este sábado desde las 18.00 horas, con las actuaciones de la Banda de Música da Comarca, Ancoradoira y Meigas e Trasgos. El pregón correrá a cargo de la panadería Pallares a las 20.00 horas y, tras la cena, llegará a la una de la madrugada el momento central: la tradicional danza de la Noite Meiga, que recrea un conjuro de desamor. Broken Peach y Miguel Fialeiro cerrarán la fiesta.

articles.headline: La inflación se dispara al 4,3% en agosto, máximo en tres años
articles.subtitle: El IPC sube siete décimas en un mes por el encarecimiento de los carburantes tras la retirada del escudo anticrisis. La subyacente cae al 2,9%, pero el Gobierno reactivará desde septiembre el descuento de 20 céntimos al diésel.
articles.body:
El Instituto Nacional de Estadística confirmó el viernes que la inflación repuntó hasta el 4,3% en agosto, siete décimas más que en julio y su nivel más alto desde febrero de 2023, cuando el shock de la guerra de Ucrania aún estaba reciente. El dato adelantado, que sorprendió al alza a los analistas, dispara las alarmas sobre una nueva crisis de precios justo al final del verano.

El principal responsable son los carburantes, encarecidos por la guerra en Irán y por el fin de la rebaja fiscal el 30 de junio: el diésel ha subido un 21% entre principios de julio y finales de agosto, y la gasolina un 13%. La inflación subyacente, que excluye energía y alimentos no elaborados, bajó una décima, hasta el 2,9%, lo que sugiere que el shock aún no se ha contagiado al resto de la cesta. Funcas, que preveía un 3,7%, advierte de que los choques energéticos que parecen transitorios pueden acabar siendo persistentes.

## Qué viene ahora

La escalada activa automáticamente la cláusula del real decreto anticrisis: desde el 1 de septiembre el descuento al diésel sube de 10 a 20 céntimos por litro, mientras la gasolina bajará a cinco. El repunte también presiona al BCE, que afronta una posible subida de tipos en septiembre, con efectos sobre hipotecas y alquileres, cuyo tope de subida anual depende en parte del IPC.

articles.headline: El Gobierno atribuye la crisis de Ceuta a los bulos y pide refuerzos a la UE
articles.subtitle: Albares sitúa el detonante de la entrada masiva en la viralización de mentiras en redes y Robles desliza amenazas híbridas, mientras Interior solicita a Bruselas agentes de Frontex y Europol para el triaje de los migrantes que quedan en la ciudad.
articles.body:
El relato oficial sobre la entrada masiva del 30 de julio, en la que entraron 72.000 personas según el nuevo dato del Gobierno, se agrieta por dentro. José Manuel Albares insistió el viernes en el Congreso en que el detonante fue la «viralización inédita de mentiras y bulos» en las redes sociales, y defendió que el papel de Marruecos fue «esencial» para frenar la crisis. Margarita Robles, en cambio, no acusó a Rabat pero tampoco lo absolvió: habló de «amenazas híbridas» que usan la inmigración con fines desestabilizadores y dijo que «el país vecino sabrá lo que ha hecho y lo que no».

La distancia entre ambos ministros alimenta las críticas de la oposición y de los socios del Gobierno, que reprochan a Moncloa no tener una única versión de los hechos y no haber pedido explicaciones a Marruecos. Sánchez comparecerá el jueves 3 de septiembre, y la gestión de la crisis apunta a ser el eje del debate.

## Refuerzos europeos

En paralelo, Marlaska ha remitido a la Comisión Europea una solicitud formal de apoyo para el triaje de los migrantes que permanecen en Ceuta: diez agentes adicionales de Frontex, la extensión de la operación Minerva y la asistencia de Europol y de la Agencia de Asilo de la UE, además de 32 millones en ayuda de emergencia solicitados la semana pasada.

articles.headline: La formación digital del Gobierno devolverá más de 200 millones a Europa
articles.subtitle: El plan de competencias digitales apenas ha ejecutado el 41% de sus 3.500 millones, según la AIReF. El programa con Unión Profesional formó a 23.500 personas, menos de un tercio de las 80.000 previstas, y los fondos sin gastar deberán volver a Bruselas.
articles.body:
Los programas con los que el Gobierno pretendía acelerar la formación digital e inteligencia artificial de los españoles encadenan fracasos y ahora abocan a devolver fondos europeos. Según la AIReF, de los 3.500 millones consignados al plan de competencias digitales apenas se ha ejecutado el 41%, y el Gobierno deberá reintegrar más de 200 millones a Bruselas.

El caso más llamativo es la subvención de 200 millones que Red.es concedió a dedo a Unión Profesional para formar a más de 80.000 colegiados. El programa, que terminó el 30 de junio, solo logró 23.500 inscritos, menos del 30% del objetivo. Este lunes vence el plazo de ejecución fijado por Bruselas, por lo que unos 120 millones volverán previsiblemente al Tesoro. La Escuela de Organización Industrial también registró renuncias por 122,7 millones, y RTVE ya devolvió unos 30 millones del proyecto Haz, cuya gestión investiga la Fiscalía Europea.

El balance general es pobre: las competencias digitales básicas han pasado del 57% al 68% de la población desde 2021, aún lejos del 80% que Bruselas marca para 2030, y los especialistas tecnológicos siguen por debajo de la media europea.

articles.headline: Entra en vigor la nueva jubilación flexible, que abre la puerta a los autónomos
articles.subtitle: La reforma aprobada en mayo permite compaginar pensión y trabajo por cuenta propia por primera vez, elimina el periodo de carencia y sube los incentivos económicos, aunque UPTA denuncia que deja fuera a quienes llegan a la jubilación siendo autónomos.
articles.body:
El real decreto que reforma la jubilación flexible entró en vigor el viernes, con el objetivo de que más jubilados sigan activos sin perder del todo su pensión. La norma, pactada en la reforma de pensiones de 2024, permite por primera vez compaginar la pensión con una actividad por cuenta propia, elimina el periodo de espera para solicitarla y amplía la jornada parcial admitida, del 25-75% al 33-80%.

Quienes se reincorporen al menos seis meses después de jubilarse cobrarán un 25% adicional de pensión con jornadas del 55% al 80%, o un 15% si trabajan entre el 33% y el 55%. En el caso del trabajo autónomo, el pensionista podrá percibir hasta el 25% de la prestación. La medida busca acercar la edad efectiva de jubilación a la legal: la demora voluntaria ha pasado del 4,8% al 10,9% de las jubilaciones desde 2021, y las anticipadas han caído del 43% al 30%.

UPTA, sin embargo, carga contra el diseño: el requisito de no haber cotizado en el RETA durante los tres años previos deja fuera, en la práctica, a quienes se jubilan siendo autónomos, a los que la asociación considera «trabajadores de segunda» del sistema de pensiones.

articles.headline: SSE Airtricity gas bills to rise by almost 19% from October
articles.subtitle: The increase hits about 204,000 domestic customers and 4,500 small businesses from 1 October, adding roughly £172 to a typical annual bill. Watchdogs blame the Middle East conflict for doubling wholesale gas prices.
articles.body:
Northern Ireland's largest gas supplier, SSE Airtricity, is raising prices by 19.2% from 1 October, adding about £172 to the annual bill of a typical household in the Greater Belfast and west gas network areas and pushing the average credit-meter bill to around £1,080. The increase affects roughly 204,000 domestic customers and 4,500 small commercial ones.

The company blames "unprecedented volatility" in global energy markets: wholesale gas prices have effectively doubled since the US and Israel began their attack on Iran, and the closure of the Strait of Hormuz has curtailed shipments through a waterway that normally carries about a fifth of the world's oil and liquefied natural gas. Colin Broomfield of the Utility Regulator said the rise would be "difficult news for many households", and the Consumer Council's Raymond Gormley warned of "a very serious situation this winter", with combined gas and electricity bills in the affected areas set to exceed £2,000 a year.

## Mitigation

Stormont is rolling out a £100 home heating oil voucher scheme next month and a discount of around £50 on electricity bills in October, which the Economy Minister is seeking to increase from £30. Fuel poverty campaigners, including DUP MLA Andy Allen, argue targeted support is now needed for gas customers so that help does not depend on how a home is heated.

articles.headline: Bryant to weigh Parades Commission's future as Orange Order demands clear-out
articles.subtitle: The Northern Ireland Secretary will study the commission's plan to restore confidence over the weekend after one member quit over the quashed Drumcree ruling. The Orange Order wants the rest to go; Sinn Féin says any parade down the Garvaghy Road is still off the table.
articles.body:
Northern Ireland Secretary Sir Chris Bryant has received the Parades Commission's letter setting out how it plans to restore public confidence and will consider it over the weekend, saying confidence in the body has "taken quite a knock" but he is "not in the business of pulling the whole thing down".

The letter was demanded after the High Court quashed this year's Drumcree determination, with Mr Justice McAlinden citing "errors", "short cuts" and "sloppy procedures" in how the commission handled the annual parade outside Portadown. Commissioner Billy Gamble, the focus of much of the criticism, resigned on Thursday, and the commission conceded it had not considered the ruling in its final form.

## Positions harden

The Orange Order is keeping up the pressure: the Grand Lodge says the remaining five commissioners must "acknowledge their failings" and follow Gamble, and Portadown District added "one down, more to go" while declaring itself "ready and willing to engage in mediation... without any pre-conditions". Sinn Féin councillor Catherine Nelson, however, dismissed that offer: talks about a parade down the Garvaghy Road, blocked since 1998, are "off the table". DUP leader Gavin Robinson said the matter is "far from resolved" and called for a review of the commission's governing legislation. Bryant has warned that losing more commissioners risks leaving the body unable to function.

articles.headline: Norway mourns King Harald V as Haakon VIII ascends the throne
articles.subtitle: Harald, Europe's oldest reigning monarch, died in hospital aged 89 after 35 years on the throne. His son Haakon VIII has taken office, with an oath before parliament due on Tuesday as the country begins a period of national mourning.
articles.body:
Norwegians are grieving the death of King Harald V, who died in hospital at 06:35 local time on Friday aged 89 after being treated for a rare blood condition. An estimated 10,000 people lined the streets of Oslo as his coffin was taken from the hospital to the royal palace in a public procession, and crowds left flowers and flags outside the palace gates.

His son, Haakon VIII, held an extraordinary council of state with ministers, adopting the royal motto "All for Norway", which dates back to his great-grandfather. His wife Mette-Marit is now queen and their daughter, 22-year-old Ingrid Alexandra, becomes crown princess. Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre said the country was "united in grief and gratitude", and the armed forces honoured the late king with a 21-gun salute from Akershus Fortress. He will lie in state in the palace chapel; no funeral date has yet been announced.

## A difficult succession

Haakon takes the throne at a turbulent moment for the monarchy. Queen Mette-Marit faced scrutiny this year over her past friendship with the late convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, and is recovering from a lung transplant, while her son from a previous relationship, Marius Borg Høiby, was convicted of rape in June. Support for the monarchy has dropped from 72% in 2024 to 54%, though royal experts say the new king is respected and hard-working.

articles.headline: Trump hails 'historic' deal giving US control of Venezuela's oil reserves
articles.subtitle: Washington says the agreement covers more than 65 billion barrels of proven reserves through a 17-field venture in which the US would hold a 55% stake under a 100-year concession. Few details have been released and its legality in Venezuela is unclear.
articles.body:
President Donald Trump has announced a sweeping agreement with Venezuela's interim president, Delcy Rodríguez, that he says gives the United States control of more than 65 billion barrels of proven oil reserves - "THE BIGGEST OIL DEAL IN WORLD HISTORY", in his words - more than doubling American reserves and, he claims, lowering US petrol prices. It was negotiated by Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth "through a partnership with private business", at "no cost to the American Taxpayer".

## Unanswered questions

According to Rodríguez, the deal covers 17 strategic oil fields with a proven potential of 65 billion barrels, more than $100 billion in investment and $209 billion in taxes for the state. A US official told CBS News that Washington would retain 55% control of a joint venture with a private operator and hold a 100-year concession - an arrangement apparently wider in scope than the US-led coalition's control of Iraqi oil revenue after 2003. The official text has not been released, and it is unclear whether the agreement could face legal and constitutional challenges in Venezuela, where Maduro was seized in a US special forces operation in January. Venezuela holds the world's largest proven reserves, an estimated 303 billion barrels, though production has collapsed since the late 1990s.

articles.headline: Iceland votes on whether to resume EU accession talks
articles.subtitle: A knife-edge referendum closes at 22:00 on Saturday with polls too close to call. Fisheries and sovereignty dominate the campaign, while Trump's interest in Greenland hangs over the debate.
articles.body:
Icelanders are voting in a referendum on whether to resume accession negotiations with the European Union, 13 years after talks were broken off. The latest opinion poll puts the No campaign ahead with 51.6%, though an earlier poll had Yes leading, and more than one in five of the roughly 265,000 eligible voters had already cast ballots before Saturday. Results are expected in the early hours of Sunday.

A Yes vote would not mean joining the EU: it would kick-start negotiations - 11 of 35 chapters were already provisionally complete when talks stalled in 2013, and officials say they could be finalised in one or two years - but any final deal would still need a second referendum, parliamentary approval and a constitutional amendment.

## Fish, sovereignty and security

The campaign has been fought less over security than over fisheries, which make up almost 40% of exports, and sovereignty. No campaigners, led by Independence Party chair Guðrún Hafsteinsdóttir, vow never to share Iceland's fishing grounds under the EU's Common Fisheries Policy - "final decisions should be made here in Iceland". Prime Minister Kristrún Frostadóttir leads the Yes side, calling membership "one of the biggest risk-reducing steps we can take". US President Donald Trump's threats to control Greenland have cast a shadow over the vote, though Iceland remains a Nato founder with no standing military, and this year signed a security and defence partnership with the EU.

articles.headline: Tim Cook hands Apple to John Ternus as the Cook era closes
articles.subtitle: Cook becomes executive chairman on Tuesday as hardware chief John Ternus, 50, takes over as CEO in Apple's first succession since Steve Jobs. Under Cook, Apple's market value grew from about $350 billion to $4.5 trillion.
articles.body:
Apple's first leadership transition in 15 years lands on Tuesday, when John Ternus, the company's head of hardware engineering, becomes CEO and Tim Cook moves to executive chairman. Cook, who took the top job weeks before Steve Jobs died in 2011, wrapped up his tenure this week with a private farewell concert at Apple Park headlined by OneRepublic in front of about 200 employees.

## The record

The numbers are historic. Apple was worth roughly $350 billion when Cook took over; it now sits around $4.5 trillion, having been the first company to reach $1 trillion (2018), $2 trillion (2020) and $3 trillion (2022), and it briefly topped $5 trillion in July. Annual revenue has nearly quadrupled to $416 billion, services revenue has grown from $9.4 billion to more than $109 billion on 1.5 billion subscriptions, and the installed base has passed 2.5 billion devices. Ternus, a 25-year Apple veteran who led the iPad, AirPods and the transition of Macs to Apple silicon, takes over with the AI race as the unfinished business: the Siri revamp promised in 2024 is two years late and Apple now leans on Google's Gemini. His first act will likely be the iPhone 18 launch, including Apple's first foldable. Cook, meanwhile, stays on to handle regulators in Washington, Brussels and Beijing.

articles.headline: Apple TV+ raises prices again: $14.99 a month, its fourth hike in four years
articles.subtitle: The streaming service jumps from $12.99 to $14.99 monthly, or $119 a year, for new and existing US subscribers, with the Apple One bundle up to $21.95. The price has tripled since the service launched at $4.99 in 2019.
articles.body:
Apple raised the price of Apple TV on Friday, its fourth increase in four years. The monthly subscription goes from $12.99 to $14.99, and the annual plan from $99 to $119, effective immediately for new subscribers, with existing ones to be notified about a month before the new rate applies. The individual Apple One tier, which bundles TV with iCloud+, Music, Arcade and other services, rises from $19.95 to $21.95.

The move comes almost exactly a year after the last increase, when the service jumped 30% from $9.99, and puts Apple TV on par with rival streamers that have also been raising rates: Netflix hiked prices in March and Peacock announced an increase earlier this month. Apple is betting the timing works, with the fourth season of Ted Lasso recently premiered, live sports like F1 and MLB on the service, and a September 9 iPhone event - expected to include its first foldable - about to dominate the news cycle.

articles.headline: Judge rules Pentagon's 'supply chain risk' label for Anthropic was unlawful
articles.subtitle: Judge Rita Lin found the Trump administration's designation was retaliation for Anthropic's safety guardrails, violating the First and Fifth Amendments. The separate D.C. case is still pending, so Anthropic technically remains labeled.
articles.body:
A federal judge in California ruled Thursday evening that the Pentagon's designation of Anthropic as a supply chain risk was illegal. In a 59-page summary judgment, U.S. District Judge Rita Lin found the label imposed in February and March - after CEO Dario Amodei refused to remove guardrails preventing the military from using Claude in autonomous weapons and mass surveillance - constituted "unlawful retaliation in violation of the First Amendment" and denied the company the due process required under the Fifth Amendment.

## The ruling

Lin wrote that the government's "words and deeds confirm that the challenged actions were based on a desire to make a public example out of Anthropic for its 'arrogance' in criticizing the government," adding that "the empty invocation of national security is not a blank check to punish and retaliate against government critics." She pointed out that Anthropic "undisputedly lacks" any backdoor access to its technology and that the Defense Department kept pursuing contracts with the company, even collaborating with its new model, Mythos, on cybersecurity. The ruling is Anthropic's first court win in the dispute, though its separate D.C. lawsuit continues - until it is resolved, the company technically remains a supply chain risk. CNBC notes the victory clears a hurdle as Anthropic marches toward a near-record IPO.

articles.headline: OpenAI cuts off Cursor after SpaceX's $60B takeover
articles.subtitle: OpenAI says it will wind down its contract with the AI coding tool - now owned by SpaceX - citing distrust of Musk's companies, with model access ending November 12. Cursor will lean harder on Anthropic's Claude and its in-house Composer model.
articles.body:
OpenAI announced Friday that it is ending its partnership with Cursor, cutting off the coding tool's access to its models on November 12 - the maximum notice its contract allows. The decision, made within a change-of-control cancellation window, comes two weeks after SpaceX closed its $60 billion all-stock acquisition of Cursor's parent, Anysphere, folding the popular assistant into Musk's SpaceXAI division.

OpenAI framed the move in terms of trust, not technology: "We cannot be confident that SpaceX will use our technology within our terms of service, based on our experience with Elon Musk's companies violating contracts," it wrote, citing X's alleged breach after the Twitter takeover and Musk's admission under oath that xAI violated OpenAI's terms. It also pointed to accountability for its upcoming model, Astra.

## What happens to developers

Cursor, used by a reported 67% of the Fortune 500 with over $1 billion in annualized revenue, will lean more on Anthropic's Claude and its in-house Composer model, trained on SpaceX's Colossus compute. The open question is whether Anthropic - which has its own multi-billion-dollar compute deal with SpaceX - makes the same call.
